Why — the human shouldn't be the trigger

Today most agents only act when a human asks. Event-driven agents act when time says so or when the world changes — a tool you operate becomes a teammate that works while you sleep.

  • Request-response caps the value — nothing happens unless someone remembers to ask, and insights expire when the chat closes.
  • The market is flooded with smart replies. The durable moat is autonomy — agents that watch, wait, and act.
  • The customer ask is shifting from “answer my question” to “keep an eye on this and tell me when it matters.”
Wake sourceExampleStatus
You ask it“what is the price of bitcoin?” live — 4 channels
The clock“every morning at 8, send me the weather” live — CRON
The world changes“ping me only when this PR / price / file changes” live — 42 triggers, POLL + PUSH

From ask → answer to watch → act

A chat agent

You ask, it answers, the conversation ends. Nothing happens unless a human types.

“summarize this PR” — once.

An event-driven agent

You arm a standing flow once. From then on the world triggers the agent — a PR opens, an email lands, a reaction is added — and the answer is delivered where you asked from.

“review every new PR on my repo” — forever.

One sentence in any channel is enough: the concierge turns natural language into an armed, standing flow — no console, no YAML.

Architecture — one seam, two backends

  • /invoke is the single seam: every trigger, from every backend, arrives as the same envelope {agent, source, event}.
  • AP backend — an Activepieces flow holds the piece trigger; AP holds the credentials. The agent never sees a token.
  • Direct backend — CUGA already receives Slack Events / the Discord Gateway, so a watcher is just a subscription row. No AP flow at all.

One agent — the supervisor model

Users and events address exactly one agent: cuga. Specialists exist, but they are its sub-agents — never addressed, never exposed.

channels / triggers / webhooks ──► /invoke {agent: "cuga", source, event}
                                        │
                              cuga (SUPERVISOR, EVENTS_SUPERVISOR=1)
                              reads its roster: supervisor_agents.yaml
                                        │  picks ONE specialist per wake-up
                                        ▼
                     27 sub-agents — a skill each: prompt · tools · HANDLES-trigger hints
                                        │  answer bubbles up
                                        ▼
                     delivered to wherever the conversation/flow originated
  • Adding a sub-agent = editing a YAML (CUGA-main's canonical supervisor schema) + make reload. No API, no deployment.
  • Channels and credentials are platform-level — a sub-agent gets event content and its own tools, never a token, never a channel identity.
  • Routing is a measured gate, not a vibe: make test-delegation scores the supervisor's picks on labelled payloads (first full run: 14/14, zero self-answers).
  • Flag unset → the same one agent, as plain classic CUGA — the whole events layer still works.

The trigger registry — one table rules everything

triggers.py holds 42 triggers — one row per (integration, event): the AP piece trigger or the direct event kind, the curated payload map, the config slots, the classifier phrases, and a synthetic fire payload.

  • flow building, classification, arm-time validation, the docs and the tests all derive from it — nothing is wired twice
  • an unknown trigger fails loudly at build time (the old code silently armed a flow that could never publish)
  • 27 triggers run via Activepieces · 15 run direct

Adding a trigger = adding one row (+ an agent that declares it). The parametrized test suite picks it up automatically.

Channels — where you talk to it (and where answers land)

webthe built-in chat — always on, zero setup
slackdirect backend: CUGA receives the Events API itself (signed HMAC)
discorddirect backend: CUGA holds the Gateway websocket
telegrambot long-poll via the events layer

The sink follows the origin: arm a watcher from Slack and the answers arrive in Slack; arm it from web chat and they ride back over HTTP. Same agent, same flow.

Two tracks that converge — channels vs. watch/act

Track A — Channels (converse)

Where a human talks to the agent: web, Slack, Discord, Telegram. This is transport plumbing — speaking each platform's API (Events API, Gateway, bot stream).

Mostly independent of the product logic. A channel can be added — or a flaky one fixed — without touching a single trigger or action. It ships on its own cadence.

Track B — Triggers + Actions (watch / act)

Where the agent value lives: watch a tool, reason, act on another. Registry-driven — adding a piece is data, not code.

This is the product. It doesn't care which channel you spoke from.

The two are decoupled by design and meet at one seam — /invoke. Any channel in, any trigger/action out. So "open up Slack/Discord/Telegram" and "support GitHub/Gmail/Calendar actions" are separate deliverables that compose — not one tangled effort.

What's built — two tracks, one seam

Track A · Channels — communication

4 channels a human converses over: web · Slack · Discord · Telegram. Two-way — you ask, the answer lands back in the same place.

This half is transport. Necessary, but it is not the product.

Track B · Events — watch / act

42 triggers across 11 integrations the agent watches, then acts on — 7 via Activepieces, 5 direct.

GitHub · Gmail · Box · Slack · Google Calendar · Pinterest · YouTube · RSS · Discord · Telegram · Webhook.

Adding a piece is data, not code — the newest four (Calendar, Pinterest, YouTube, RSS) landed as registry rows + a synth sample, then armed live.

Both meet at /invoke. Test any event with no connection via POST /api/events/synth-fire; connect Calendar/Pinterest via OAuth for the real fire. YouTube + RSS need no OAuth (public feeds).

From watch → act: the action half

A trigger fires the agent — then the agent's answer drives a real action in a connected app, as a step in the same flow. Not just notify: do.

Say it like thisAction armedStatus
“when I get an email, draft a reply summarizing my response”gmail/create_draft_replylive
“when an email arrives, reply to the sender with a short acknowledgement”gmail/reply_to_emaillive
“when I get an email, email me a summary at me@example.com”gmail/send_emaillive
“when I get an email, email me a summary at me@example.com and reply to the sender”gmail/send_email+gmail/reply_to_emaillive
  • Gmail is the live pilot — reply to the sender, draft a reply, send a fresh email; multi-action (“email me AND reply”) and N-way branching (“if urgent reply, else draft”) all arm as valid Activepieces flows.
  • Registry-driven — an action is a data row generated from the live AP catalog. Adding GitHub/Slack/Calendar actions is data, not engine code.
  • Three anti-silent-failure gates — deterministic build · an arm-time AP validity gate (an invalid step is refused, never a false “ARMED”) · an LLM verifier that flags intent mismatches. A 22-case NL→Flow benchmark holds CORRECT-AT-ARM at 100%.

Direct triggers can act too — the executor (Option A)

Slack / Discord / Telegram triggers own no Activepieces flow (CUGA receives them itself), so their Gmail action runs via a reusable executor flow CUGA fires after the agent answers — Activepieces still keeps the credentials.

Say it like thisAction armedStatus
“when a message is posted in #alerts, email me a summary at me@example.com”gmail/send_emailoffline
“when someone posts in #general on discord, email me a summary at me@example.com”gmail/send_emailoffline
“when the telegram bot gets a link, email me a summary at me@example.com”gmail/send_emailoffline
  • One general mechanism unlocks slack/discord/telegram → gmail — no per-channel code.
  • Live-verified: the full arm path + executor creation + Activepieces validity gate (which caught two real bugs while proving it). Pending: the executor run hits an Activepieces platform error — the send doesn't execute on the test instance yet.
  • Never silent — if the action can't be armed, the concierge declines and says why.

Creating a flow — one sentence, or one command

Natural language (any channel)

“when a PR is opened on psf/requests, review it and post a summary”

The concierge classifies the sentence → resolves the trigger in the registry → validates the config (asks for missing slots like the repo) → arms the flow. Re-asking reuses the existing flow (dedup), never duplicates it.

Slash commands

/automate <what> — the router picks cron / poll / push for you.
/cron · /poll · /push · /watch — force a specific kind.

POST /api/events/hook/{name} — external systems fire a webhook; either way it lands on the one agent (cuga), whose supervisor picks the right specialist internally.

NL→Flow — engineered, not vibes

The contract: a sentence becomes exactly the right flow, or a question — never silently the wrong flow. Two fuzzy hops, everything else deterministic:

1 · A deterministic pre-router first

Registry-generated phrases classify the trigger; slots (repo, label, folder…) are extracted from the sentence. HIGH confidence demands a standing-flow marker, ONE distinct app, and no foreign vocabulary — then it arms without an LLM call, instantly.

Ask-till-legit: a missing required slot becomes ONE question; the next message fills the blank (“acme/api” → armed). A topic-change reply is never crammed into the slot.

2 · The LLM for genuine ambiguity

Anything the pre-router won't claim goes to the concierge LLM, whose prompt carries the registry's full trigger vocabulary. Its proposal still passes the same validation gate — an unknown trigger or missing slot comes back as a question, never a broken flow. Both doors arm through one code path: connect gate → dedup (DB unique index) → build.

Benchmarked in CI: 56 hand-labelled cases (utterance → expected FlowSpec) — fast-path 43/46 push cases (93%), correct-at-high 43/43, gated on zero wrong-at-high. It caught two real bugs on its first run. Full walkthrough: events_docs/nl_to_flow.html.

How we know it works — two levels of benchmark

Arming a flow is not proof it works. A flow can compile perfectly and still never fire, or fire down the wrong branch. So we benchmark at two levels — a capability is "done" only when it passes both.

 Level 1 · NL → APLevel 2 · Execution
QuestionDid we build the right flow? Does the flow actually work?
Runs againstfake engine — offline, deterministic real Activepieces + real connections
Whenevery commit (CI)nightly / pre-release
Assertsmode · trigger · action · gate outcome valid+enabled → fires → right step ran → effect verified in the app → delivered
MetricCORRECT-AT-ARM (56 cases, 100%) FIRE-RATE · EXECUTION-CORRECT · EFFECT-VERIFIED
Statusexists building — validity gate + --check + synth-fire today

Fire strategy is tagged per trigger: synth (github webhooks, machine-fireable) · real (a controllable local action — box upload, a slack message) · manual (a real email — a scripted send in the harness). Level 2 is what turns "armed" into "proven."

Under the hood — the technical highlights

LayerWhat it doesFuzzy or deterministic?
The envelope API POST /invoke {agent, source, event} + gateway token — ONE contract for every wake source: 4 chat channels, 27 AP piece triggers, 15 direct watchers, webhooks, cron/poll. New wake source = new caller, zero new agent code. deterministic
NL→Flow (arm time) the concierge COMPILES a sentence: kind (cron/poll/push) → trigger (registry phrases) → slots extracted → validated → deduped (DB unique index) → AP flow built. Missing slot = ONE question; the next message fills it (ask-till-legit). deterministic fast path; LLM only for genuine ambiguity — gated on zero-wrong-at-high (56 labelled cases in CI)
Routing (fire time) the supervisor reads the event payload + its roster's HANDLES hints and picks one specialist; the answer bubbles up. Hints are generated FROM the trigger registry — they cannot drift. one LLM inference per wake-up — measured by make test-delegation
Execution each sub-agent = a full CUGA agent (canonical SDK), tools scoped to its declared MCP servers; AP resolves credentials in its sandbox and delivers CONTENT, never tokens. deterministic wiring
Delivery the sink follows the origin — answers land in the channel (thread) the request or flow came from; direct channels are sent by CUGA itself, no AP send step. deterministic

The division of labor in one line: language is compiled at arm time, judgment is spent at fire time, and everything either side of the LLM is a function you can test.

The receipts — why you can trust this

  • One registry, zero drift. All 42 triggers live in one table; flows, classifier, validation, docs, this deck and the tests derive from it — and five golden gates fail the build if any generated page goes stale.
  • Live-fired, not just armed. All 14 GitHub triggers arm as real AP flows with real repo webhooks and fire with real agent answers (91s harness). A real human's 🐛 reaction in Slack fired the incident agent end to end. The harnesses distinguish ARMED from FIRED — and say so.
  • We read the vendor's compiled source. Two bugs in Activepieces' own GitHub piece (sample data its own filters would discard) — found by reading the bundled JS, pinned by tests so an upgrade can't silently regress us.
  • Security by construction. OAuth tokens live only in AP's encrypted store; CUGA passes connection names. OAuth state is HMAC-signed and expiring. Every CUGA-held secret resolves through vault:// aws:// db:// URIs.
  • Races are refereed by the database. Flow identity is a canonical dedup key under a unique index — two simultaneous asks produce one flow, deterministically.
  • Honest verdicts everywhere. The test vocabulary separates PASS / XFAIL / ARMED / NOFIRE / SKIP — a green that means “exists” is never sold as “works”.
  • One agent, measured routing. Users and events address ONE agent — cuga, a supervisor whose specialists load from a canonical YAML roster. Its per-event routing is a gated benchmark (make test-delegation): first full run 14/14, zero self-answers.

Credentials — the agent never holds a token

  • Activepieces is the vault: OAuth tokens live encrypted in AP's own store; flows resolve them inside AP's sandbox. CUGA passes a connection name, never a secret.
  • Per-user vs shared: each integration on an agent declares its credential ownership — per-user (everyone logs in) or shared (one service account).
  • The secret seam: every CUGA-held credential (bot tokens, AP password, gateway token) resolves through vault:// aws:// db:// env:// URIs — plaintext still works in dev.
  • Signed OAuth state: connect callbacks carry an HMAC-signed, expiring state — a forged or replayed callback is a hard reject.

Multi-tenant cloud — the isolation gate (v2)

Can one hosted CUGA serve many users, each with their own integrations — my Gmail vs. your Gmail — with no data leak? The design says yes; the runtime isn't there yet. Today: single-user / trusted-demo. Multi-user cloud is v2.

What already holds up (the design)

  • Per-user connections: each user's token is a distinct AP connection ea::<tenant>::<user>::<app>, encrypted, never seen by the agent.
  • One flow per user: flows are scope-namespaced and the connection is baked in at arm time — you cannot accidentally run user B's flow on user A's token.
  • Channels isolate via the link-token handshake; principal threads per request.

What breaks under real multi-user load

  • No auth identity on the web path → every browser user collapses to user_id="local" → shared connection → cross-user Gmail leak. The dominant gap.
  • ActivityTracker is a process-global singleton (core CUGA) → concurrent runs corrupt each other's intent / steps / screenshots.
  • EVENTS_DB=":memory:", box-direct single-token, AP one-project CE degrade.

Critical path to safe: inject X-User-Id from auth · durable EVENTS_DB · contextvar-scope the tracker (upstream). All fixable — full analysis in events_docs/DEPLOYMENT_ISSUES.md. Naming the gate is how we ship v1 honestly.

Proven end-to-end — live, not mocked

  • Offline gate (make test) — every registry row parametrized: flow building, classification (a labelled utterance per trigger), validation, dedup, signed state.
  • live_github_triggers.py — arms all 14 GitHub triggers as real AP flows with real repo webhooks, fires each synthetically, asserts a real agent answer, cleans up.
  • live_direct_watchers.py — fires HMAC-signed Slack Events API callbacks through the same verification a genuine delivery passes.
  • Real events — a real Slack reaction, a real Box upload and comment, real Gmail arms: verified through the full loop, answer delivered back into the channel.
  • make test-fire — the only harness that waits for a genuine schedule tick: ARMED is not FIRED, and the verdicts say which.

Roadmap — tight, sequenced, quality-first

Don't chase breadth. Make the core undeniable, then extend. Four priorities, in order:

#PriorityWhat it means
1NL → Flow The product's front door. Harden the sentence→flow compiler: ambiguity handling, ask-till-legit slot-filling, the LLM-verify seam — one sentence must become the RIGHT flow or a question, never silently the wrong one.
2Benchmarking Two levels. L1 NL→AP (did we build the right flow?) — have it. L2 execution (does it FIRE → run the right action → produce the real effect?) — build it. Armed ≠ works.
3Harden what we have The 7 integrations + Gmail/GitHub actions already in place — take each to Level-2 green, live-vetted end to end. Close the known bugs. Depth over new logos.
4Extend Only then add pieces — Calendar · Sheets · Outlook · Slack/Discord actions. Each is registry data, not engine code; the gates + Studio + this deck update themselves.

Discipline: a capability is "done" only when it passes both benchmark levels. Full plan: events_docs/roadmap.html · gaps: events_docs/todos_actions/GAPS.md
